title: Endocrine and Reproductive Physiology (PIO 301/303)
description: Hormone mechanisms, the hypothalamus and pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreatic and calcium-regulating hormones, and male and female reproductive physiology.

topics.title: Hormone Action and the Hypothalamic–Pituitary Axis
topics.summary: Classes of hormones, receptors and second messengers, feedback, and pituitary hormones.

notes.b: Peptide hormones (insulin, glucagon, ADH, ACTH) and catecholamines are water-soluble and act on cell-surface receptors via second messengers: cAMP (Gs/Gi — e.g. glucagon, ACTH, TSH, β-adrenergic), IP3/DAG and Ca2+ (Gq — e.g. α1, oxytocin, GnRH) or receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin, growth factors). Steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, oestrogen, testosterone) and thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble and act on intracellular receptors to alter gene transcription, so their effects are slower. Most endocrine systems are regulated by negative feedback.
k: Steroids and thyroid hormones: intracellular receptors

notes.b: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) through releasing hormones in the hypophyseal portal system: TRH → TSH; CRH → ACTH; GnRH → FSH and LH; GHRH → GH (somatostatin inhibits GH); dopamine inhibits prolactin. The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) stores and releases ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. Excess growth hormone causes gigantism before epiphyseal fusion and acromegaly after; deficiency causes short stature. A prolactinoma causes galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Pituitary stalk compression raises prolactin (loss of dopamine inhibition).

topics.title: Thyroid Hormones
topics.summary: Synthesis, regulation and actions of thyroid hormones, hypo- and hyperthyroidism.

notes.b: Thyroid follicular cells trap iodide (Na+/I− symporter), which is oxidised and attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase (inhibited by carbimazole and propylthiouracil) to form MIT and DIT, which couple to form T4 (thyroxine, most secreted) and T3 (triiodothyronine, more active). T4 is converted to T3 in tissues by deiodinases. Most circulating hormone is bound to thyroxine-binding globulin. TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates all steps; T3/T4 feed back negatively on TSH and TRH. Parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin.
k: T4 secreted mainly; T3 more active
TSH stimulates; T3/T4 feed back negatively

notes.b: Thyroid hormones increase basal metabolic rate, oxygen consumption and heat production, enhance β-adrenergic sensitivity (tachycardia), and are essential for normal growth and brain development in infancy. Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, dry skin, menorrhagia; congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) causes intellectual disability — prevented by newborn screening and by iodised salt. Hyperthyroidism (commonest cause Graves' disease — TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies): weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia/atrial fibrillation, exophthalmos. In primary hypothyroidism TSH is high; in primary hyperthyroidism TSH is suppressed.
k: Hypothyroid: cold intolerance, weight gain; TSH high
Iodised salt prevents goitre and cretinism

topics.title: Adrenal Hormones and Stress
topics.summary: Cortisol, aldosterone and adrenal androgens; adrenal medulla; Cushing's and Addison's disease.

notes.b: The adrenal cortex has three zones ('GFR — salt, sugar, sex'): zona glomerulosa (aldosterone — regulated mainly by angiotensin II and potassium), zona fasciculata (cortisol — regulated by ACTH) and zona reticularis (androgens such as DHEA). Cortisol raises blood glucose (gluconeogenesis), promotes protein catabolism, suppresses immunity and inflammation, and is needed for vascular response to catecholamines; it follows a circadian rhythm, highest in the early morning. Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to retain Na+ and water and excrete K+ and H+.
k: Cortisol peaks in the early morning

notes.b: Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol — commonly from steroid therapy; Cushing's disease is ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma): central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis and proximal myopathy. Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency, often autoimmune or TB in Nigeria): fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyperpigmentation (high ACTH), hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia; an Addisonian crisis is life-threatening. Conn's syndrome (aldosteronoma) causes hypertension with hypokalaemia. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline; a phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.
k: Cushing's: moon face, striae, hypertension, hyperglycaemia
Addison's: hyperpigmentation, low Na+, high K+

topics.title: Pancreatic Hormones and Calcium Regulation
topics.summary: Insulin and glucagon, diabetes mellitus, and PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin.

notes.b: The islets of Langerhans contain α cells (glucagon), β cells (insulin), δ cells (somatostatin) and PP cells. Insulin is released when glucose enters β cells via GLUT2, raising ATP, closing K-ATP channels (the target of sulphonylureas), depolarising the cell and opening Ca2+ channels. Insulin promotes glucose uptake into muscle and fat (GLUT4), glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis, and drives K+ into cells (used to treat hyperkalaemia). Glucagon raises blood glucose through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune β-cell destruction (absolute insulin deficiency, risk of DKA); type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance with relative deficiency and is linked to obesity. Diagnosis: fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), random ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms, or HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol).
k: Glucose → ATP → K-ATP closes → insulin release
Insulin: GLUT4, glycogen, fat, K+ into cells

notes.b: Normal serum calcium is about 2.2–2.6 mmol/L; about 45% is ionised (the active form). Parathyroid hormone (PTH), released when calcium falls, raises calcium by increasing bone resorption, increasing renal Ca2+ reabsorption and phosphate excretion, and stimulating renal 1α-hydroxylase to form calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D). Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Calcitonin lowers calcium (minor role in humans). Hypocalcaemia causes tetany (Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs), which may follow thyroidectomy with accidental parathyroid removal; hypercalcaemia ('bones, stones, groans and moans') occurs in hyperparathyroidism and malignancy.
k: Hypocalcaemia: tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs

topics.title: Reproductive Physiology
topics.summary: Male reproductive hormones, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, parturition and lactation.

notes.b: In males, LH stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone; FSH with testosterone stimulates Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and secrete inhibin (which feeds back on FSH). In females the menstrual cycle (average 28 days) has a follicular phase (FSH drives follicle growth; rising oestrogen), ovulation (triggered by the LH surge around day 14 — a positive feedback effect of high oestrogen), and a luteal phase (the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and oestrogen; lasts a fairly constant 14 days). The endometrium shows proliferative (oestrogen) and secretory (progesterone) phases; menstruation follows progesterone withdrawal. Progesterone raises basal body temperature by about 0.3–0.5 °C after ovulation.

After implantation, hCG from the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production (about 8–12 weeks). The placenta also secretes oestriol, human placental lactogen (insulin resistance) and relaxin. Labour involves positive feedback: stretch of the cervix triggers oxytocin release (Ferguson reflex), increasing contractions. Prolactin (from the anterior pituitary) stimulates milk production, while oxytocin causes milk ejection (let-down) in response to suckling. High oestrogen and progesterone in pregnancy inhibit lactation until after delivery. Lactational amenorrhoea results from suppression of GnRH by prolactin.
